deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE TABLES ARE (my identification; the page has no text). Every modulus is a prime p ≡ 5 (mod 8): 5, 13, 29, 37, 53, 61. For each of these, 2 is a primitive root. That explains why 17 and 41 are skipped.

LEFT 4×4 TABLE. Put f = (p−1)/4. Partition the residues 1..p−1 into four biquadratic classes C_k = {x : ind_2(x) ≡ k mod 4}, k = 0..3, with index taken to base 2. Split the interval (0,p) into four quarters I_j = (j·p/4, (j+1)·p/4), j = 0..3. The entry in row k, column j is
N(k,j) = #{x in C_k : x in I_j}.
This is the distribution of the biquadratic residue classes over the four quarters of the modulus.

Verification (mine). For p = 13, with g = 2:
- C0 = {1,3,9}
- C1 = {2,5,6}
- C2 = {4,10,12}
- C3 = {7,8,11}
- I0 = 1..3, I1 = 4..6, I2 = 7..9, I3 = 10..12.
This gives rows (2,0,1,0), (1,2,0,0), (0,1,0,2), (0,0,2,1), exactly Gauss's table.

For p = 29: C0 = {1,7,16,20,23,24,25} gives (2,0,2,3), and C1 = {2,3,11,14,17,19,21} gives (2,2,3,0); both match.

I recomputed row 0 (and row 1 where noted) for the other primes:
- 37: row 0 (3,3,1,2), row 1 (1,3,2,3)
- 53: row 0 (3,3,2,5), row 1 (2,3,5,3)
- 61: row 0 (5,4,2,4), row 1 (2,5,4,4)
- 5: the permutation table (1→C0, 2→C1, 3→C3, 4→C2)
All agree with the manuscript. Row and column sums are all f, because each class and each quarter has f elements.

STRUCTURE. Write row 0 as (a,b,c,d). In every case the table is
(a,b,c,d) / (c,a,d,b) / (d,c,b,a) / (b,d,a,c).

Rows 2 and 3 are forced. Since p ≡ 5 (mod 8), −1 = 2^{2f} lies in C2, and x → p−x maps I_j to I_{3−j}. Hence N(k+2,j) = N(k,3−j).

The relation row1 = (c,a,d,b) is not forced by any obvious symmetry. Using x → 2x it reduces (my derivation) to identities of the type #C0∩(0,p/8) = #C0∩(5p/8,3p/4). It holds for all six primes; Gauss may have been probing exactly such regularities.

RIGHT 2×4 TABLE. Its rows are row0+row2 and row1+row3. This is the distribution of quadratic residues (C0∪C2) and non-residues (C1∪C3) over the four quarters. Each row has the pattern (x,y,y,x), by the −1 symmetry. The values are:
- 5: 1001 / 0110
- 13: 2112 / 1221
- 29: 5225 / 2552
- 37: 5445 / 4554
- 53: 8558 / 5885
- 61: 9669 / 6996 (only '9 6 / 6 9' written)

CLASS-NUMBER CONNECTION (my observation). The difference x − y, i.e. residues minus non-residues in the first quarter, is 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 3. This equals h(−4p)/2, since h(−20)=2, h(−52)=2, h(−116)=6, h(−148)=2, h(−212)=6, h(−244)=6. That is Dirichlet's formula Σ_{0<n<p/4} (n/p) = h(−4p)/2 for p ≡ 1 mod 4. The left table refines this quadratic count to the biquadratic level.

CONTEXT. The surrounding pages deal with the biquadratic character of 1+i (supplementary law) and biquadratic reciprocity (the 'Dec.' table). The marginal '1−i, 1−i' suggests the tables were made while seeking a criterion, Gauss-lemma style via quarter counts, for the character of 1±i or of 2. The 'x' marks at 13 and 53 have no evident meaning that I could determine.
errors: No numerical errors found. Every recomputed row agrees: all rows for 5, 13 and 29 (rows 2–3 via the forced −1 symmetry), and rows 0–1 for 37, 53 and 61.
The 2×4 table for 61 is left incomplete (only '9 6 / 6 9'); its full form would be 9 6 6 9 / 6 9 9 6.

results.what: Table of the number of elements of each biquadratic class (index mod 4 to primitive root 2) in each quarter (jp/4,(j+1)p/4) of the modulus, for p = 5, 13, 29, 37, 53, 61 (all ≡ 5 mod 8).
results.modern_name: Distribution of quartic residue classes in quarter intervals (quartic analogue of counting quadratic residues in (0,p/4)); related to Jacobsthal/Gauss-sum evaluations
results.usually_credited_to: Systematic results: Berndt & Evans (1970s, 'Sums of Gauss, Eisenstein, Jacobi, Jacobsthal and Brewer', 1979) and others; the quadratic case goes back to Dirichlet (1839)

results.what: Observed structure: the table is determined by row 0 (a,b,c,d) as (a,b,c,d)/(c,a,d,b)/(d,c,b,a)/(b,d,a,c). Rows 2–3 follow from −1 ∈ C2; row 1 is a nontrivial empirical regularity.
results.modern_name: Symmetry relations among quartic interval counts

results.what: Quadratic residues versus non-residues in each quarter (the right-hand table); its first-quarter excess equals h(−4p)/2.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet's class number formula for character sums over (0,p/4)
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet 1839 (Gauss is known to have had class-number/character-sum relations unpublished)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely numerical, with no stated theorem. Still, it shows Gauss explicitly tabulating how the biquadratic classes are distributed across the quarters of the modulus. This is a quartic refinement of the residue-in-intervals counts connected with class numbers, studied systematically much later (Berndt–Evans era). The data also exhibit a nontrivial regularity (row1 = permutation of row0). It is notable as an unpublished exploratory detail, but there is no explicit result.
